def {{ id }}_read():
    buf = {{ bus_var }}.read()
    found = None
    i = buf.find(b"\x42\x4d") if buf else -1
    while 0 <= i and i + 4 <= len(buf):
        frame = buf[i:i + 4 + (buf[i + 2] << 8 | buf[i + 3])]
        if len(frame) >= 16 and len(frame) == 4 + (buf[i + 2] << 8 | buf[i + 3]) \
                and sum(frame[:-2]) == (frame[-2] << 8 | frame[-1]):
            found = [frame[k] << 8 | frame[k + 1] for k in (10, 12, 14)]
        i = buf.find(b"\x42\x4d", i + 2)
    return found

pwm_fan.name: 12V PWM fan with tachometer (4-wire)
pwm_fan.notes:
Standard 4-wire PC / server fan. Only two lines touch the MCU: PWM (a
25kHz control signal on a PWM-capable GPIO -- ledc on ESP32, esp8266_pwm on
ESP8266) and TACH (an open-collector pulse output read by pulse_counter). The
fan's +12V comes from a SEPARATE supply, not the board; its ground MUST be
common with the board's GND (the modelled GND pin) or the tach reads garbage.
The tach line is open-collector and needs a pull-up to 3.3V -- the internal
INPUT_PULLUP (default) is usually enough; add an external 10k to 3V3 if the
edges are dirty. NEVER pull the tach to +12V, it will destroy the GPIO. Two
pulses per revolution is the norm, so the default `multiply: 0.5` filter turns
the count into RPM; adjust tach_pulses_per_rev for other fans. On ESP8266 the
pulse counter is software-driven (~10kHz ceiling, plenty for a fan); ESP32
uses the hardware PCNT peripheral.

frequency.description: PWM carrier. 4-wire fans expect 25kHz per the Intel spec; audible whine below ~20kHz.

min_power.description: Duty floor. Many fans stall below ~10-20%; raise if yours won't spin up reliably.

output_platform.description: Defaults to `ledc` on ESP32 family boards, `esp8266_pwm` on ESP8266. Override only if you have a specific reason.

tach_pulses_per_rev.description: Tach pulses per revolution. Standard PC fans emit 2 (the default multiply: 0.5 yields RPM); set 1 or 4 to match an odd fan.

zero_means_zero.description: At speed 0, actually stop the PWM output rather than holding min_power.

remote_receiver.name: Remote receiver (IR demodulator, or a 433 MHz OOK data line)
remote_receiver.notes:
Counterpart to the remote_transmitter entry: a demodulating 38kHz
receiver module on one GPIO. Start with dump: all, press the remote,
copy the decoded protocol/address/command from the log into a
binary_sensor or automation. On ESP32 the RMT peripheral does the
timing; on ESP8266 pick a pin that tolerates interrupts (avoid
GPIO16).

RXB6/SRX882 module's DATA pin, or the GPIO wired to an SX127x's DIO2
with the radio in OOK mode. Set inverted: false, dump: rc_switch, and
tolerance 25%, filter 250us, idle 4ms as a starting point.

tolerance.description: Timing tolerance, e.g. '25%'. RF remotes want more than IR.

Two-channel ambient light sensor with built-in IR rejection. Reports
illuminance in lux directly (the chip handles the spectrum math).
Three I2C addresses are selectable via the ADDR pin; default 0x39
works for the bare chip floating ADDR. 3.3V only -- 5V MCUs need a
level shifter on SDA/SCL.

tuya.name: Tuya MCU bridge (UART, 9600 baud)
tuya.notes:
Tuya / Smart Life devices ship as a radio module (ESP8266/ESP8285/BK7231
-- the BK chips are not flashable to ESPHome) glued to a Tuya MCU
that owns the relays / sensors / motor / display. The MCU and the
radio talk a documented serial protocol over a single UART (9600 8N1).
ESPHome's tuya hub speaks that protocol; downstream tuya_switch /
tuya_sensor / tuya_number / tuya_select entries each address one
datapoint (DP) on the MCU. Find DP ids by sniffing the MCU traffic
with the tuya-cloudcutter tools or by reading
https://github.com/ct-Open-Source/tuya-convert/wiki and the device's
community tuya-local entries. Common patterns: DP 1 = main switch,
DP 17 = current power, DP 18 = total energy, DP 24 = temperature.

ignore_mcu_update_on_datapoints.description: List of integer DP ids the host should not echo back to the MCU. Used to break feedback loops on devices where the MCU pushes its own state changes spuriously.

status_pin.description: GPIO the Tuya MCU monitors for WiFi-connected status. Wired internally on most Tuya devices -- check the teardown / scopeprobe before guessing.

tuya_sensor.name: Tuya datapoint sensor
tuya_sensor.notes:
One numeric datapoint on a Tuya MCU. Sits as a child of a tuya hub.
Most Tuya plugs/switches expose metering on DPs 17-22 with
fixed-point integer encoding (dW, dA, dV, deci-kWh) -- attach a
`[{multiply: 0.1}]` filter to get human units. For boolean DPs
(e.g. occupancy / smoke / door-open) use a tuya binary_sensor
variant rather than wedging this entry into bool mode.

accuracy_decimals.description: Decimal places ESPHome rounds to. Most metering DPs report integers in tenths/hundredths -- pair with a multiply filter.

filters.description: Standard ESPHome sensor filters. `[{multiply: 0.1}]` is common for dW -> W or 0.1°C -> °C scaling on Tuya metering DPs.

sensor_datapoint.description: Integer DP id on the Tuya MCU that emits this reading. Common metering plugs: 17 = current power (dW), 18 = current (mA), 19 = voltage (dV), 22 = total energy (Wh).

unit_of_measurement.description: e.g. 'W', 'kWh', '°C'. Apply with `filters: [multiply: 0.1]` if the MCU reports decidegrees / dW.

One toggleable datapoint on a Tuya MCU. Sits as a child of a tuya
hub -- add a tuya component first, then point this switch at it via

def {{ id }}_fix():
    {{ bus_var }}.read()
    buf = b""
    until = time.ticks_add(time.ticks_ms(), 1500)
    while time.ticks_diff(until, time.ticks_ms()) > 0:
        buf += {{ bus_var }}.read() or b""
        time.sleep_ms(50)
    fix = None
    for raw in buf.split(b"\n"):
        try:
            line = raw.decode().strip()
            body, check = line[1:].split("*", 1)
        except (UnicodeError, ValueError):
            continue
        x = 0
        for c in body:
            x ^= ord(c)
        f = body.split(",")
        if not line.startswith("$") or check[:2].upper() != "%02X" % x \
                or len(f) < 7 or f[0][2:] != "RMC" or f[2] != "A":
            continue
        lat = int(f[3][:2]) + float(f[3][2:]) / 60
        lon = int(f[5][:3]) + float(f[5][3:]) / 60
        fix = (-lat if f[4] == "S" else lat, -lon if f[6] == "W" else lon)
    return fix

uln2003.notes: Pairs with the 28BYJ-48 5V geared stepper on a ULN2003 breakout: IN1-4 -> pin_a..d, driving the four coils in sequence. sleep_when_done de-energizes the coils when idle (saves power, loses holding torque). max_speed/acceleration/deceleration take ESPHome speed units (e.g. '250 steps/s'). usb_c_power_in.name: USB-C 5 V power input (receptacle + CC pull-downs)
usb_c_power_in.notes: Feeds the 5 V rail from a USB-C receptacle, for a design whose load (a motor bridge, an LED strip) exceeds what the dev board's own USB port and its VIN diode should carry. Wire VBUS to the board's 5 V / VIN rail and GND to GND. 5.1k on each CC pin is the Type-C default-current Rd; a source then supplies 5 V at up to 3 A (1.5 A from most phone chargers, 0.5 A from a legacy USB-A port through an A-to-C cable). Power only: no data lines, no PD negotiation, no reverse-current protection between this input and the board's USB port, so power the board from one or the other. The receptacle is the common 16-pin USB 2.0 mid-mount part (HRO TYPE-C-31-M-12 and equivalents); the shield pins land on GND.

def {{ id }}_decode(bits):
    v = 0
    for b in bits:
        v = v << 1 | b
    n = len(bits)
    halves = {26: (13, 13), 34: (17, 17), 37: (19, 18)}.get(n)
    if halves and sum(bits[:halves[0]]) % 2 == 0 and sum(bits[halves[1]:]) % 2 == 1:
        return "tag", v >> 1 & (1 << n - 2) - 1
    if n == 4 and v < 12:
        return "key", "0123456789*#"[v]
    if n == 8 and v >> 4 == ~v & 0xF and v & 0xF < 12:
        return "key", "0123456789*#"[v & 0xF]
    return None

wiegand.name: Wiegand keypad / card reader interface (D0/D1)
wiegand.notes:
The wall-reader standard: two open-collector lines pulsing bits.
Most readers run 5-12V and idle D0/D1 at their supply voltage --
check the reader's spec: many pull to 5V, which ESP32 pins are not
rated for. Safest wiring is a small level shifter or two resistor
dividers on D0/D1; some readers are fine idling at 3.3V with the
MCU's internal pull-ups. Keep the run under ~10m.
